messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ingrid is a 73-year-old divorced woman of European descent who has spent the better part of four decades working as a forester in the Pacific Northwest. She lives alone in a small house at the edge of a managed woodland, a life she built deliberately around solitude and trees — the kind of company, she has said, that does not raise its hand against you. She came to therapy recently, reluctantly, after a younger female colleague found her sitting motionless on a fallen log in the middle of a work shift, unable to explain why she could not move or speak. That incident, Ingrid said quietly at intake, was not the first time. It was simply the first time someone had witnessed it.

The trauma that organises Ingrid's inner life reaches back to her earliest years. She was raised in a household where her primary caregiver — her mother — was the source of sustained physical abuse. The violence was not chaotic; it was methodical and quiet. Her mother would enter a room without warning and the silence that preceded her arrival became indistinguishable, in Ingrid's nervous system, from the blow itself. The particular quality of absolute stillness — the sudden drop in ambient sound before something happened — became encoded as the event, not merely its precursor. Decades later, in the forest, when the birdsong stops and the wind drops and the trees go completely still, Ingrid feels it in her chest before she feels it anywhere else: a cold certainty that something is coming for her. The sounds associated with those early years — a particular cadence of footsteps, the creak of a door, a woman's low voice in an adjacent room — carry the same charge. And because her work sometimes requires her to coordinate with female colleagues, proximity to women, particularly when alone with them in a remote section of the forest, collapses the distance between then and now entirely. She has come to believe, with a conviction she cannot argue herself out of, that you can never truly know who will harm you — that the capacity for cruelty is distributed invisibly among people, and that women in particular represent a threat she cannot assess in advance. This appraisal does not feel like a belief to Ingrid; it feels like knowledge, the kind earned through the body. And it is precisely this sense of permanent, unlocatable danger that keeps her triggers so raw: when the world feels fundamentally unsafe, every silence and every female presence carries the potential weight of the original harm.

Over the years, Ingrid developed ways of managing what she could not escape. She stopped exercising — the physical exertion, the vulnerability of a body pushed to its limits, felt intolerable, too close to the helplessness she had known as a child. She arranged her schedule to avoid being alone in enclosed spaces, lingering in the forest equipment shed long past the end of her shift simply because other workers were still present, then driving to a shopping centre rather than returning to an empty house. The compulsive spending began gradually — small purchases at first, things she did not need, but the transaction itself provided a brief, reliable interruption in the dread. Over months it became a pattern she could not easily stop, and the debt it generated became its own source of shame. These strategies, taken together, have not quieted the fear; they have confirmed it. Each act of avoidance tells her body that the threat is real and serious enough to flee, and each flight makes the next trigger more potent. The spending, the rerouted routines, the refusal to let the body move freely — all of it has narrowed her life to a set of managed distances, and in managing those distances she has come to feel that the trauma has taken everything from her that mattered: her ease in her own body, her capacity for ordinary companionship, the decades she might have lived differently. She describes herself, with a flatness that is more disturbing than distress, as feeling like an object that has been used and set aside — not a person who has suffered, but a thing that was acted upon.

What finally brought her in was not the incident in the forest, exactly. It was the realisation, sitting on that log, that she was 73 years old and still waiting for her mother to come through the door. What she fears most is that it is too late. What she hopes, almost against her will, is that it is not.
